1343-bureaucracy:
Honoré de Balzac turns his satiric eye on the French civil service in this novel of clerks, chiefs, and promotions. In a government office, rival officials scheme for a vacant post, while wives, patrons, and petty jealousies decide who rises and who rots at a desk.

Balzac writes office life with the same detail he gave to salons and counting houses, and his clerks are comic and all too human. The novel is a sharp portrait of red tape and ambition. It suits readers who like Balzac's Paris and the comedy of work.
1410-the-commission-in-lunacy:
Balzac's tale opens in Paris in 1828, when a famous doctor and a lawyer leave a great house near the Elysee at one in the morning. Their errand concerns a marquis whose family seeks a commission in lunacy, a legal finding that would strip him of control over his fortune and his life.

Behind the legal forms lies a struggle over money, marriage, and a mind said to be unsound, with doctors, kin, and lovers pulling in rival directions. Balzac treats the case as both mystery and satire. The result is a sharp, compact study of how law and family can conspire against one man.
1421-mrs-lirriper-s-legacy:
Mrs Lirriper, a London lodging-house keeper, tells this Christmas story in her own chatty voice. Left a small legacy, she sets out on a journey she never planned, carrying her lodger's hopes with her, and she meets kindness, muddle, and surprise at every stop along the road.

Told as a fireside ramble, the tale moves from her own easy chair to strange towns and new friends, and back to the lodgings she loves. Its charm is Mrs Lirriper herself: plain-spoken, warm, and funny. Readers meet a woman whose good sense steadies everyone around her.
1990-the-bedford-row-conspiracy:
William Makepeace Thackeray sets this short comic tale in a small town split by two rival factions, where love and local politics pull the same strings. Mr. Perkins loves Miss Gorgon, but family pride and party feeling stand in the way. Thackeray wrote the tale early in his career, when he was learning satire in magazines and short fiction.

Thackeray, working from a plot by Charles de Bernard, builds the fun from gossip, scheming, and scenes behind the scenes. The story is brief and satirical, poking at snobbery and small-town power with a light hand. The small-town factions mirror London party strife in miniature, which is the joke Thackeray keeps returning to.
20394-correspondence-relating-to-executi:
In the Ottoman Empire, leaving the Muslim faith could be punished by death. This volume prints official letters about executions in Turkey for apostasy from Islam. British officials wrote home as they tried to stop the killings.

One letter tells how a diplomat used all his influence to turn the Porte from its course. He acted for the sake of a distracted family, whose tears and pleas moved him, and because serious politics hung on the case. His efforts failed. The papers show how religion, law, and foreign pressure collided in the empire.
21510-legacy:
Trigger Argee, ace agent of the Old Galactic League, stars in James H. Schmitz's science fiction novel Legacy. The book first appeared as A Tale of Two Clocks, and Schmitz also wrote The Witches of Karres. It opens near a training school, with a quiet range and an empty parade ground.

On a city street, spacers on leave crowd round Trigger and clap a hand over her mouth. An aircar lifts her away in a smooth, expert snatch. From that grab grows the mystery of her whole life, tied to old alien finds and League plots. Schmitz writes fast, wry space adventure with a sharp heroine.
22461-union-and-democracy:
Allen Johnson wrote Union and Democracy, a history published in 1915. It traces American political growth after independence was won. Johnson opens with the young nation's buoyant economic expectations.

Once assured of independence, Americans faced their future confidently. As colonizers of a new world, they trusted their own strength. Freed from the British mercantile system, they felt no doubt. They expected to compete for the markets of the world. From that confidence, Johnson follows union and democracy forward. The book suits its wartime moment of national self-examination. Readers get early twentieth-century history writing: clear, patriotic, and focused on institutions and trade.
5871-green-fancy:
McCutcheon's Green Fancy opens on a highway where the first wayfarer and the second wayfarer meet and part. A solitary figure trudges along a narrow road winding through dismal, forbidding forest depths, weary and footsore yet swift and resolute in advance. Night comes on, bringing uncertain prospects of shelter, and the wayfarer's journey toward a place called Green Fancy begins.

It offers a romantic adventure of roads, forests, and a mysterious house, told with McCutcheon's polished charm. The novel favors suspense, disguise, and love over realism, letting a night road lead to unexpected company. Fans of early twentieth-century romance will enjoy its brisk opening, and new readers will find an easy, engaging tale of a traveler and a green fancy.
6460-problems-in-american-democracy:
Thames Ross Williamson, assistant professor of economics and sociology at Smith College, writes Problems in American Democracy as growing pains of civilization, offering chances for personal achievement and national progress. National greatness, he opens, means substantial contributions to civilization, a well rounded, highly developed culture of material and social well being. Egypt's hieroglyphs, Greece's art and literature, Phoenician navigation, and Roman law and architecture show how diverse such contributions can be.

Italy, France, and other European nations advanced music and painting, while America faces its own problems in turn. A mid passage cites due process: no citizen deprived of life, liberty, or property without it. It notes Kansas in 1920 creating a Court of Industrial Relations to preserve public peace, protect health, and prevent industrial strife. Williamson writes a textbook of civic problems, hopeful that problems point the way forward.
6921-temporal-power-a-study-in-supremacy:
Marie Corelli sets this novel in a kingdom where crown and church contend for mastery, as its subtitle, a study in supremacy, warns. The contents name a king's pleasance, sealed orders, a nation's choice between church and state, and a king's double. Sergius Thord, idealists, a premier's signet, and a sea princess move through chapters on corruption, royal lovers, and a vote for love.

Later chapters turn to secret service, a king's veto, a morganatic match, and a song of freedom, closing with abdication. Corelli writes in her grand romantic manner, with courts, priests, and patriots in sharp contrast. The tale asks whether a king serves his people, his church, or his own heart.
7129-the-prospective-mother-a-handbook-f:
J Morris Slemons, associate professor of obstetrics at Johns Hopkins University, writes The Prospective Mother as a handbook for women during pregnancy. Aimed at women with no special medical knowledge, it answers questions that occur in the course of pregnancy. Detailed directions for safeguarding health stress measures that may prevent serious complications. Treatment of such conditions is not discussed, since only a physician observing the individual patient can judge it.

Slemons stresses that notable improvement in childbirth care depends on not waiting for untoward symptoms before consulting a physician. Prospective mothers must learn to be under a doctor's care early, not merely in crisis. The book is a plain, careful guide to a safe pregnancy, written before modern obstetrics yet sound in its counsel.
bureaucracy:
Honore de Balzac's Bureaucracy, translated by Katharine Prescott Wormeley, opens in the Rabourdin household in Paris. Xavier Rabourdin, forty, gray-haired, and head of a bureau in an important ministry, has drafted a reform that would shrink the civil service and reward merit. His wife Celestine backs the plan with social ambition.

Against him conspire clerks, deputies, and the cashier who explains the customary outfit indemnity skimmed for ministers' households. Balzac anatomizes office intrigue, dossiers, and dinner-party warfare with insider relish, even dropping into script form for one office scene. The novel, part of his Scenes from Political Life, remains the classic fiction of administration, funny because its clerks' battles are deadly serious to them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexandre-de-:
Alexandre de Prouville, Marquis de Tracy, was Viceroy of New France, born in France in 1603 of noble parents and dead there in 1670. A soldier from youth, he proved his valour in many battles and rose to lieutenant-general. Louis XIV gave him wide mission and jurisdiction over all French possessions in the New World. He redeemed Cayenne from the Dutch, restored order in the Antilles, and reached Quebec in 1665.

With Governor Courcelles and Intendant Talon, Tracy opened a glorious period in New France. To secure the colony's peace, war was decreed against the Agniers. Despite his age Tracy led the invading army, having built three forts on the Richelieu the year before, including Sorel and Chambly. The Agniers fled, sued for peace, and asked for missionaries, and Tracy then organized courts of justice and promoted farming and industry. The first horses seen in Canada arrived under his administration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anne-first-du:
Anne de Montmorency, born Chantilly 1492, died Paris 1567. His family had been first Barons since 1327. Educated with the future Francis I, he was made marshal in 1522 for Novara, and freeing the Pavia prisoner won favour. He became grand master and Governor of Languedoc. His cleverness won the Cambrai treaty in 1529, releasing Francis I's sons; his power was unlimited. His new policy: France should regain strength.

The truces of Nice and the 1538 treaty were his work. Constable since 1538, he was disgraced in 1541. In 1547 Henry II recalled him; in 1551 he became duke. Opposed to the Guises, he still sought peace. His Catholic convictions led him with Guise to a triumvirate for Catholicism. Wounded and captured at Dreux, he later joined Condé at Havre. In the second war of religion, a follower mortally wounded him at Saint-Denis. Of indomitable courage, his cruelty shocked. He preferred defensive warfare and worked for absolutism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-annecy:
Haute-Savoie makes up the diocese of Annecy, except Alby and Rumilly parishes, which belong to Chambery, together with the canton of Ugenes in Savoie. Chambery is its metropolitan see. Geneva's exiled bishops lived at Annecy from 1535 to 1801. Saint Francis de Sales served as Annecy's bishop from 1602 to 1622.

Between 1801 and 1822, Annecy belonged to Chambery and Geneva, then became an episcopal see in 1822 by the bull Sollicita catholici gregis. Saint Bernard of Menthon, founder of the Grand Saint Bernard hospice, is still honoured at Annecy. In 1610, Saint Francis de Sales and Saint Jane Frances de Chantal founded the Visitation at Annecy; at the foundress's death it numbered 87 convents. Annecy's Visitation Church preserves their relics. Near Lac d'Annecy, the ancient Benedictine abbey of Talloires lends picturesqueness to the scene. At the end of 1905 the diocese counted 267,496 inhabitants across 29 first-class parishes and 270 second-class parishes, plus 167 vicariates, formerly with state subventions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-thomas-per:
Blessed Thomas Percy, Earl of Northumberland and martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1528, eldest son of Sir Thomas Percy, he died at York in 1572. His father was executed at Tyburn in 1537 for the Pilgrimage of Grace, and the boy was taken from his mother and raised by Sir Thomas Tempest.

Restored in blood by Parliament in 1549, Percy rose to the earldom and led the Northern Rising of 1569 for the old faith and Mary, Queen of Scots. Captured after the rising failed, he was beheaded at York, refusing to save himself by changing religion. The entry presents a nobleman martyr of the northern rebellion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-william-la:
Blessed William Lacy, a martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Yorkshire, he suffered at York on 22 August 1582. His wife was the widow Cresswell, mother of Arthur and Joseph, later Jesuits, and held a paid Crown post, possibly as coroner, until about 1565. Fourteen years a widower, he went abroad for the priesthood and returned to Yorkshire ministry.

Arrested and held at York Castle from July 1582 in heavy irons and an underground dungeon, he was arraigned in August and condemned with Richard Kirkman, a fellow missionary priest. The two shared a turret cell until Kirkman's removal to a dungeon, and both died together. The entry presents a late vocation ending on the scaffold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brothers-of-o: The Brothers of Our Lady of Mercy were founded at Mechlin in 1839 by Canon Scheppers; they teach and tend prisoners and the sick. Cardinal Pecci, later Leo XIII, saw their work as nuncio at Brussels, invited them to Saint Balbina in Perugia, and had Pius IX confirm them in 1854. Manning brought them to London in 1855, where they care for prisoners in Catholic reformatories and teach children. They live under simple vows, spend one year as novices, and wear a habit and scapular with a brown cross.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brothers-of-t:
The Brothers of the Holy Infancy, founded in 1853 by John Timon, first Bishop of Buffalo, care for destitute and wayward boys and seek their own sanctification. Timon bought land at West Seneca, now Lackawanna, and built Saint Joseph's Male Orphan Asylum and Saint John's Protectory. Thomas Hines ran the struggling houses under heavy debt until Nelson Baker took charge in 1882.

Baker placed the work under Our Lady of Victory and founded her society for destitute Catholic children, and the work prospered. Today's Our Lady of Victory Home groups a protectory of 700 boys, an orphan asylum of 250, a working boys' home of 75, and an infant asylum of about 150. Twenty-three brothers teach trades from printing and baking to plumbing and tailoring, and the bishop governs through a priest superior.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-dem:
An entry on Christian Democracy, whose name and reality, it warns, have very different histories. The reality was defined by Leo the Thirteenth in Graves de communi as popular Catholic action. That means an organised movement with a set programme for the people's pressing problems, popular in the sense of the fourth estate, the plebs, and Catholic in leadership and lines. Not everything Catholics do for the people counts under that strict sense.

The germ lies in Christianity itself and in the Church's mission, and from Constantine onward clergy worked practically for the people's well-being. The entry traces that tradition, then the modern name's career as a school and a political party, noting how partisans bent the term from its encyclical meaning. It closes at the chronicle stage, pointing readers to Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, and Spain for national stories.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-civil-aspect-:
Bankruptcy, from the Latin bancus, bench, and ruptus, broken, means the wreck of a trader's business. The English statute of 1542, against persons who make bankrupt, gave creditors a summary way to share a fleeing or housekeeping debtor's assets. A statute of 1570 then defined the bankrupt debtor more closely and limited the remedy to traders.

Bankruptcy law and insolvency law differ in motive. Insolvency law relieves debtors from imprisonment and other penalties. Bankruptcy law relieves creditors against dishonest debtors, even ones who might not be insolvent. The article also treats business failures in the mass, reading crises such as Hamburg in 1799 and England in 1814 as symptoms of a deeper commercial disease, not mere individual misconduct.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corporal-and-:
Joseph Delany's entry treats the corporal and spiritual works of mercy. Saint Thomas Aquinas teaches that although mercy springs from charity, it still counts as a special virtue, distinct from charity. The Scholastics refer it mainly to justice, since it governs relations between distinct persons, ad alterum.

Its motive is misery discerned in another, particularly insofar as the condition seems involuntary. The corporal works are feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, harbouring the harbourless, visiting the sick, ransoming the captive, and burying the dead. The spiritual works are instructing the ignorant, counselling the doubtful, admonishing sinners, bearing wrongs patiently, forgiving offences willingly, comforting the afflicted, and praying for the living and the dead. Christ states the command in the most stringent terms, and failure brings eternal damnation. For ransoming captives, the sixth corporal work, two religious orders devoted themselves to redeeming slaves.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-illegitimacy:
Illegitimacy, in the usual sense used here, is the state of a child born outside marriage. Roman law and canon law, though, turned such a child legitimate if the parents later married. Many European states took up that rule, while England and most American states did not.

The condition is likely far more widespread, frequent, and steady than most people think. No figures exist to measure it in the United States and Canada. Tables in the entry give, for leading European countries over the past thirty years, what share of live births were illegitimate. They draw on Krose and the Statesman's Year Book for 1908, with Austria, Belgium, Denmark, and England and Wales among the cases.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-percy:
John Percy, alias John Fisher, was an English Jesuit controversialist who disputed before James I. Born at Holmeside in Durham in 1569 and converted at fourteen, he studied at Reims and Rome and entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1594. He set out for England in 1596, only to be seized by the Dutch, tortured, and shipped as a prisoner to London, from which he escaped to join Father Gerard's adventures.

Seized at Harrowden at the Gunpowder Plot in 1605, he was banished at Spain's request and led the English Jesuits in Belgium. He taught Scripture at Louvain and returned to face imprisonment and a death sentence in 1610. When James I wanted disputations in 1622, Percy, then in a London prison, defended the Catholic side before the king and Laud. The debates converted the Countess of Buckingham and Chillingworth. Released in 1625, he stayed in London until his death in 1641.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-de-jou:
Joseph de Jouvancy was a French Jesuit poet, teacher, and historian who lived from 1643 to 1719. Born in Paris, he joined the Society of Jesus at sixteen, taught grammar and rhetoric at Compiègne, Caen, and La Flèche, and became professor at the College Louis-le-Grand. In 1699 his superiors called him to Rome to continue the order's official history.

Jouvancy wrote about ten tragedies, Latin and Greek poems for special occasions, and translations of French works into Latin. His school editions of Latin authors, revised for classroom use with learned notes, were reprinted in France and abroad. The entry notes that some dramas ascribed to him may belong to other Jesuits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maurice-chaun:
Maurice Chauncy, prior of the English Carthusians at Bruges, died there on 2 July 1581. His birth date is unknown. Eldest son of John Chauncey, he may have studied at Oxford and Gray's Inn before entering the London Charterhouse. In 1535 most Carthusians refused the oath of supremacy, but Chauncy, by his own account, took it.

After the monastery's surrender in 1537, he joined the Sheen Carthusians at Bruges. He returned to Sheen under Mary and was elected prior in 1556. The community fled again to Bruges in 1558, then to Louvain in 1578 under Calvinist pressure. Chauncy wrote histories of the Carthusian martyrs of Henry VIII's reign, works in which he often grieved over his own weakness in taking the oath.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-missionaries-:
The Missionaries of St. Francis de Sales of Annecy fulfil a wish St. Francis long cherished, to found a society of missionary priests. It found realization only nearly two centuries after his death. At that time Monsignor Rey, a successor of the saint in the See of Annecy, broached the idea to Father Mermier, who had been pondering the same design.

Father Mermier put the plan into execution, and in 1830 the institute was formed, with La Feuillette as the site of the mother-house. The house was solemnly blessed by the bishop on 8 August 1837, and the congregation was canonically instituted soon after. Its priests, known as the Fransalians, preach missions and retreats in the spirit of their gentle patron.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moral-aspect-:
Bankruptcy raises a moral question as well as a legal one, since sound morality requires debts to be paid. The bankrupt declares he cannot pay in full as debts fall due. Modern law no longer punishes him with slavery or prison. It seizes his property and shares it among creditors. If that covers all debts, justice and conscience are satisfied.

When creditors receive only part of what they are owed, they have suffered loss. The bankrupt bears moral blame if his own fault caused it. Living beyond his means, careless or reckless business conduct, or gambling away money owed to others all count as fault. Misfortune without fault carries no such blame. The entry weighs restitution duties, the force of a legal discharge in conscience, and when a discharged debtor must still repay.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nancy:
Nancy is a French diocese covering Meurthe and Moselle, suffragan of Besancon, heir of the celebrated see of Toul. Saint Mansuetus, apostle of the Leuci and first Bishop of Toul, cannot predate the fourth century, though some call him a disciple of Saint Peter. His successors' dates often cannot be fixed.

Among Toul's bishops stand Saint Auspicius about 470 and Saint Ursus, from whom Clovis in 496 sought a teacher of Christianity. Saint Gerard also ranks among them. Saint Gauzelin reformed Saint Epvre and founded Bouxieres, and Bruno of Dagsbourg later became Saint Leo IX. Cardinal John of Lorraine held twelve sees and six great abbeys. The entry follows Toul into Nancy, its bishops, abbeys, parishes and schools down to modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-necromancy:
Necromancy, from Greek words for dead and divination, is divination by evoking the dead. As nigromancy, black, its Italian, Spanish and old French form, it suggests black magic, where marvellous results come through evil spirits, while white magic works by human dexterity and trickery. The practice assumes the soul survives death, the disembodied spirit holds superior knowledge, and the living can communicate with the dead.

Times, places and rites of that communication varied with beliefs about the departed soul, its abode, and its ties to earth and its former body. Since divinities were often heroes raised to godhood, necromancy, mythology and demonology intertwine, and oracles of the dead blur with oracles of the gods. Found in every ancient nation, the practice is traced through pagan lands, Scripture's prohibitions, and the Church's condemnation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-papacy: The papacy is a cross-reference entry that defines the term in two senses rather than treating it at length. In its church sense it names the system in which the pope, as heir of Saint Peter and Vicar of Jesus Christ, rules the Catholic Church as supreme head. In its historical sense it names papal sway viewed as a political force in history. Readers are sent on to the entries on the Apostolic See, Apostolic Succession, the Church, Papal Arbitration, the Pope, and Unity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-primacy: Primacy, from Latin primatus, from primus, first, is the pope's supreme episcopal jurisdiction. It belongs to him in his role as the Universal Church's pastor and governor. The word marks first place, and the entry states the pope's governing office over the whole Church in a single line. No other bishop holds such jurisdiction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-privilege-of-:
A cleric's competency is his right to proper sustenance. When a parish church is joined to a collegiate house or monastery and a vicar is set over the parish's souls, the benefice holders must pay him the needful salary. No agreement can kill this right: a private deal to take less binds not the contracting vicar's successor. 

The right also holds when several simple benefices join a parish church. If the endowment falls short of the pastors needed, recourse lies to firstfruits, tithes, and collections among parishioners. The bishop must see that soul carers are duly kept. By the privilege of competency, a debt laden cleric's goods cannot be seized or sold without leaving him enough to live on. He loses the privilege, though, if he fraudulently runs up needless debts, abusing the privilege.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prophecy:
Prophecy, as mystical theology uses the word, covers both canonical Scripture's prophecies and private prophecies. In its strict sense it means foreknowledge of future events. St Paul, writing on prophecy in 1 Corinthians 14, does not fence it to future predictions, but counts in Divine promptings over what is secret, future or not.

Prophecy here means, in its strict and proper sense, the revelation of future events. Prophecy joins knowledge with the showing of what is known. That knowledge must be supernatural, breathed in by God, since it treats things past created mind's natural power. It must be shown by words or signs, since prophecy's gift serves chiefly others' good, and so needs showing. It is a Divine light showing things of the unknown future to the prophet's mind, pictured somehow, for him to show to others.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-public-honest:
Public honesty, also called decency, is a marriage impediment in canon law that makes a wedding null. This encyclopedia entry explains that it arises from a valid betrothal, or from a church-approved marriage that was never consummated. The persons caught by it may not marry each other, since their close intimacy could expose them to incontinence if marriage were open to them.

Roman law shows the older roots of the rule. Modestinus held that in entering wedlock, what is eminently fitting must be observed as well as what is lawful. So affinity from a valid marriage, consummated or not, barred marriage in the direct line without limit, and to the second degree in the indirect line. The entry works through the cases, including a man betrothed to several women related in the first degree, and cites Gasparri and Slater among the standard manuals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-de-cou:
Robert de Coucy was a medieval French master-builder at Reims, following his father in the trade. Some accounts give his birthplace as Coucy rather than Reims; he died at Reims in 1311. In 1263 he succeeded Hugues Libergier as director of the church of Saint-Nicaise at Reims, building its choir chapels and part of its transept between then and 1279. The church, begun in 1229 and ranked among the finest Gothic churches of its age, was later destroyed in the Revolution.

After his father's death, the younger Coucy also took chief charge of Reims Cathedral, rebuilt after fire in 1210. Its choir, built by his father, was finished in 1241. The cathedral's simple plan, vast choir, and narrow nave won praise from Viollet-le-Duc for strength without heaviness. Effigies of both Coucys once appeared in the nave's labyrinth, and the younger man's gravestone called him master of Notre-Dame and Saint-Nicaise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-ch:
The Sisters of Charity of Our Lady, Mother of Mercy, began in Holland in 1832. John Zwijsen, pastor of Tilburg, founded the congregation with Mary Leijsen to teach children and to aid people left without spiritual care after the Reformation. The See of Utrecht had stood vacant for about three hundred years, and the new sisters worked among a neglected Catholic population.

Their houses spread across the Netherlands, running homes for the aged and infirm, the blind, and those unable to speak, as well as hospitals. Gregory XVI approved their rules in 1843, and Pius IX approved the congregation in 1848. During a cholera outbreak their work won decorations from King William III. By December 1907 they counted 2,621 professed members in 102 houses, with about 54,300 schoolchildren enrolled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-me:
The Sisters of Mercy began in Dublin in 1827, founded by Catherine Elizabeth McAuley, born 29 September 1787 at Stormanstown House, County Dublin. She aimed to join Carmelite silence and prayer with the active labours of a Sister of Charity. The early community took the name Sisters of Mercy in 1828, making works of mercy its distinctive mark, and chose a black dress with a white collar and lace cap.

The associates unanimously chose to become a religious congregation rather than secularize. They bound themselves to instruct the ignorant, visit the sick and imprisoned, and manage hospitals, orphanages, and homes for distressed women. After opposition to joining contemplative and active life, several sisters trained with the Presentation Order, and Catherine McAuley began her novitiate at George's Hill, Dublin, that September.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-lucy:
Lucy of Syracuse, virgin martyr of 13 December, won her mother's cure at Agatha's shrine before her own death. Born of rich, noble parents about 283, her father of Roman origin died early, leaving her to her mother Eutychia, whose name suggests Greek stock. Lucy had vowed her virginity to God and hoped to give all worldly goods to the poor. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 follows the traditional story to Catania.

Her mother, less single-minded, was persuaded to pilgrimage to Catania, where Agatha, executed fifty-two years earlier under Decius, drew visitors and miracles. Eutychia hoped for cure of a haemorrhage suffered for several years, and there she was in fact cured. That cure freed Lucy to pursue her generous resolutions, and her own martyrdom followed in the traditional account. Latins and Greeks alike keep her feast on 13 December.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-defect-of:
Birth outside lawful wedlock as a bar to holy orders is the canon law topic of this entry. Illegitimate, in canon law's precise sense, means born out of lawful wedlock. Such birth blocks reception of orders and bars exercise of orders already received, though it touches liceity, not validity, and reaches even first tonsure. Only functions proper to clergy fall under the ban.

Early ages knew no such law, and illegitimate men faced exclusion only for real or supposed bad life. Urban II, 1088 to 1099, barred ordination of clerics' illegitimate offspring unless they joined approved orders. Poitiers under Paschal II, 1099 to 1118, widened the ban. Dispensations, legitimation, and later softening complete a careful guide to a stern rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-fathers-o:
Missionary priests called Fathers of Mercy, founded to save France's faith, are the congregation traced here. Lyons first housed them in 1808, Paris in 1814, and Gregory XVI approved them on 18 February 1834. Founder Jean-Baptiste Rauzan, born at Bordeaux on 5 December 1757, dying at Paris on 5 September 1847, taught theology and sacred eloquence, then served as Bordeaux's vicar-general.

There he launched a missionary drive to keep faith alive in France. Cardinal d'Aviau's word sent him to Cardinal Fesch at Lyons, who welcomed the plan, and Rauzan gathered zealous, noted preachers in 1808. Troyes preaching won even Napoleon I's favour and unsought government subsidies for missions, short-lived when Napoleon's quarrel with Pius VII broke the spell.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theocracy:
Rule by God himself, through accredited representatives, defines theocracy in this entry on civil government. Commonwealth laws stand as God's commandments, promulgated and expounded by priests or others claiming to speak for the invisible Deity. Civic duties thus form part of religion, absorbing the state into the Church or at least setting Church above state.

Josephus apparently coins the term, explaining Jewish organisation to Gentile readers against monarchies, oligarchies, and republics. Moses, he writes, ordained government by ascribing power to God and persuading the people to regard him as author of all good things. Jewish, medieval, and modern examples test how far any state truly matched the ideal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodicy:
Justification of God in the face of evil, from Greek theos and dike, is the problem Leibniz named theodicy. His 1710 Essais de Théodicée, on God's goodness, human freedom, and evil's origin, argued that worldly evil does not clash with divine goodness. Despite its many evils, this world ranks best of all possible worlds, he claimed. Bayle's scepticism forms the foil. 

Pierre Bayle, in his Historical and Critical Dictionary, denied God's goodness and omnipotence because of earthly suffering. Leibniz answered Bayle directly, and later philosophers borrowed the title for their own treatises on evil. Existence and attributes of God, optimism, and free will all enter a thorough treatment, making theodicy a gateway to philosophy of religion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vacancy:
Vacancy is the state of an office or position left without an incumbent, such as a vacant benefice, bishopric, parish, or professorship. Vacancies arise by the holder's own act or by compulsion. Broadly, any cleric, even the pope, may resign for just reasons, with resignation taking effect when duly accepted by the competent superior. Since the pope has no superior, Celestine V, who gave up the papacy, issued a special constitution.

That constitution declared the College of Cardinals competent to accept a pope's formal abdication. Under set conditions and with proper approval, an exchange of benefices or offices is allowed. Certain acts, lawful or not, count as tacit resignation, such as accepting promotion to another office. The entry sets out the canon law of vacancies with care and brevity.
doe-osti-17084200-room-temperature-singl: Swapping a photon's color at room temperature got its DOE report, and this text covers the nitrogen-gas trick. The pages detail the quantum method. The physicists get their converter. The converter was molecular. The color was swapped. The trick was nitrogen.
doe-osti-17152720-developments-regarding: Model mismatch in big physics codes got its DOE developments, and this report covers discrepancy in modular multi-physics systems. The pages detail the advances. The modelers get their update. The systems were modular. The update was discrepancy. The physics were multi.
doe-osti-2586983-evaluation-of-dna-extra: Squeezing DNA out of algae got its lab test, and this DOE report compares the kits. The pages rank the extraction winners. The biologists get their protocol. The algae were diverse. The winners were ranked. The kits were compared. The test was lab.
doe-osti-2588997-field-evaluation-of-the: HEDS got its museum field test, and this DOE evaluation covers the Timken Museum installation. The pages detail the measurements. The HVAC folks get their data. The museum was Timken. The art was Timken Museum. The folks were HVAC. The data were HVAC.
doe-osti-3030298-software-tools-ecosyste: STEP got CY2025-annualled, and this DOE software report covers the ecosystem. The pages detail the project findings. The computing folks get their data. The report was annual. The data were computing. The CY2025 were ecosystem. The annual were report.
doe-osti-3281150-multi-university-center: CUWP got multi-university-centered, and this DOE text upcycles waste plastics. The pages detail the chemical findings. The chemists get their data. The plastics were waste. The data were chemist. The CUWP were center. The waste were plastics. The chemical were upcycling.
doe-osti-3374763-a-high-power-density-an: Traction drives got density-powered, and this DOE text covers segmented inverters. The pages detail the high findings. The engineers get their data. The efficiency was power. The data were engineer. The axial were radial. The inverter were segmented. The power were high.
doe-osti-3378615-submittal-of-the-final-: NNSS got post-closure-monitored, and this DOE final CY 2025 covers letters. The pages detail the submittal findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The report was letter. The data were nuclear. The security were Nevada. The 2025 were CY. The letter were monitoring.
doe-osti-3388187-guidance-on-epact-secti: EPAct got 707-guided, and this DOE guidance covers emergency exclusions. The pages detail the repair findings. The transport folks get their data. The vehicles were restoration. The data were transport. The 707 were section. The restoration were vehicles. The emergency were exclusions.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBISecrecy_FBI_:
George Lardner Jr. reported for the Washington Post on a secret the FBI kept about secrecy itself. President Clinton's 1995 executive order set up automatic declassification of old records. The Bureau held an undisclosed blanket exemption from that order, and defended it by pointing to 6.5 million cubic feet of commingled files.

An exemption no one announced meant the order's promise stopped at the FBI's door. The Bureau argued its files were too mixed to release on schedule. Lardner's article preserves the disclosure of that carve-out, a case study in how declassification policy bends in practice.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cybervau:
During the 1960s and 1970s the National Security Agency kept watch on American citizens, a practice later called questionable in official reviews. William Burr edited this briefing book, number 605, published in September 2017. It draws on the agency's own biographic files.

NSA files covered some 73,000 United States citizens. Names included civil rights leader Ralph David Abernathy, actor Donald Sutherland, and journalists Art Buchwald and Tom Wicker. Women's Liberation and Vietnam Veterans Against the War appeared as watched groups. The record shows how a foreign intelligence agency turned its tools inward during years of protest.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
American nuclear nonproliferation policy under Presidents Nixon and Ford, from 1969 to 1977, is the subject of this Archive collection. It details that history in newly declassified documents. Those years cover the early life of the Nonproliferation Treaty and several national programs moving toward bombs.

A documentary history of a single policy lets readers watch choices accumulate: which programs drew pressure, which drew patience, and how the rules were enforced unevenly. The Nixon-Ford years set patterns that later administrations inherited. For students of proliferation, a bounded collection like this is more usable than scattered files, because the through line of one policy stays visible.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
October 2018 brought an electronic briefing book from the National Security Archive. Its subject is a side of the Cold War often left out of the story: the times the United States and the Soviet Union worked together. The editors frame the end of that rivalry as a rare, almost magical moment in world affairs.

Cooperation between rivals is the theme the records are chosen to show. Diplomats and scholars, the Archive notes, will keep studying and arguing over that ending for ages. For readers, the value lies in seeing declassified papers used to make a case. The Cold War's close, the papers suggest, owed as much to joint work and summit trust as to pressure and military strength.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_southern:
In September 1980, the American embassy in Buenos Aires sent the State Department a six-page cable with a blunt title: The Tactic of Disappearance. An August 2016 National Security Archive release is built around records of that kind. It shows how United States diplomats reported Argentina's machinery of kidnapping and secret murder while the dictatorship was still in power.

Cables like this one matter because they fix knowledge in writing, dated and signed, years before the junta fell in 1983. They undercut later claims that outsiders could not have known. For readers, the release is a window into embassy reporting at its best. Officers on the ground name a crime plainly, in real time, for a government that often preferred quieter language.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Cyber: The Office of the Director of National Intelligence publishes statistical transparency reports. They give yearly counts of how often American intelligence agencies use their surveillance powers. They also count the targets and queries those powers touch, and the secret court's rulings. A National Security Archive cyber brief presents those reports in its Cyber Vault collection. The numbers matter because they are nearly the only figures the public gets on programs described only in general terms. Readers tracking surveillance oversight will find the brief a doorway to the official statistics.
green-fancy:
Green Fancy, by George Barr McCutcheon, is a mystery romance of 1917 from the author of Graustark. McCutcheon's contents promise two wayfarers who meet and part on a highway, a man named Rushcroft who dissolves while a Mr Jones intervenes, and an extraordinary chambermaid attached to a midnight tragedy. A farm boy tells a ghastly story, and an Irishman enters, before the tale settles into its haunted country house.

Later chapters chase spun gold hair and blue eyes through various encounters, a note, some fancies, and an expedition in quest of facts. The wayfarer hero walks into an isolated estate where guests vanish, servants lie, and a beautiful prisoner seems to be held behind green shutters of rumor. McCutcheon mixes his Graustark formula of disguised royalty and American pluck with a detective plot, at the speed of a magazine serial.
love-romances-of-the-aristocracy:
Love Romances of the Aristocracy is another popular history by Thornton Hall. Hall, a barrister, filled the book with tales of Britain's great families. The picture facing the title page shows Elizabeth, Duchess of Hamilton. Chapters promise a princess of prudes, a wicked baron, and a merry duchess.

Stories here include the romance of the Villiers and a sixteenth-century elopement. There are tragedies of the turf and a ghostly visitant. Hall writes of elopements, scandals, and grand love affairs of past centuries. His manner is light and gossipy, meant for pleasure reading. The book pairs with his tales of Europe's royal courts.
maintaining-health-formerly-health-and-e:
Maintaining Health, once called Health and Efficiency, is a health manual by R. L. Alsaker. Alsaker was a doctor who also wrote Eating for Health and Efficiency. His mottoes come from Marcus Aurelius and Hippocrates: 'Nature Cures.' Early chapters treat mental attitude and the meaning of health.

Food takes up the heart of the book, chapter by chapter. Alsaker warns against overeating and sorts foods by kind. He tells readers what to eat, when to eat, and how to eat. Flesh foods get their own careful treatment. His system trusts nature over drugs and doctors. The book served the natural health movement of its day.
mrs-lirriper-s-legacy:
Charles Dickens wrote this Christmas tale, here in the 1894 Christmas Stories edition. Mrs. Lirriper, a lodging-house keeper, tells the story herself. Chapter one finds her sunk in her easy chair, out of breath. She rants at stairs, builders, and bad chimney pots.

Her chatty voice carries the whole piece, warm and wandering. V1 says the tale turns on a legacy left to her adopted boy Jemmy. Found family, not blood, is the heart of the story. Dickens mixes tears and jokes in her voice. It was a holiday favorite, and its kindness still reads as genuine and earned.
nasa-tm-19710014685-effect-of-radiometri:
D R Buchele of the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland studied errors in measuring exhaust gas temperature without touching the flow. The spectral scanning method reads gas radiation and transmission at two or more wavelengths. Fixed instruments sit outside the jet or rocket stream. From those readings, staff compute the temperature pattern across the stream.

Buchele asked how a small light reading error grows into a temperature error. That growth depends on the profile shape, path length, and gas absorption traits. He derived the conditions that keep temperature error smallest. Under good conditions, the temperature error stays near the light reading error. Short paths call for widely spaced wavelengths.
our-day-in-the-light-of-prophecy: William Ambrose Spicer's Our Day in the Light of Prophecy, copyrighted in 1917, reads the modern age through Bible prophecy. The hosted sample shows the title pages and the start of a contents list only. The contents promise a prophetic outline of world history. They also promise the second coming of Christ and signs of the approaching end. The Lisbon earthquake of 1755 gets its own chapter. No chapter text appears in the sample.
podcast-dannyjones-Kqq4_EV01cY:
Hector Berrellez was a DEA agent who investigated the murder of fellow agent Enrique Camarena, and he has argued for years that the CIA struck a secret deal with Mexican drug lords. On Danny Jones's podcast, the retired agent lays out his case, including the claim that American intelligence protected traffickers who funded its wars.

Berrellez speaks from inside the most sensitive investigation in DEA history, and his accusations have been disputed by the agencies he names for decades. Jones lets him build the timeline witness by witness. The episode's power is the source: not a theorist but the case agent himself, still prosecuting his theory in public. Listeners can weigh his record against the official findings, which cleared the CIA, and decide what a decorated agent's persistence is worth.
problems-in-american-democracy:
Thames Ross Williamson, a teacher of economics and social science at Smith College, built a textbook around the live questions of American life rather than the machinery of rule. His preface says students should meet real defects and duties before they study how government is built.

The course starts with the history and promise of American democracy, then surveys the nation's economic life as the base of its troubles. Questions of fair dealing in work and wealth take a large share of the book. Students get problems to argue, readings to test, and training for the duties of citizens.
psychology-and-industrial-efficiency:
Hugo Münsterberg, a Harvard psychologist, argued that laboratory mind science could guide hiring and work design in a book printed by Houghton Mifflin in 1913. He notes that the volume reshapes, rather than translates, his German book on psychology and economic life.

Contents move from the claims of applied psychology to finding the best possible man for each job, guiding young people to fit work, and testing the new scientific management. Münsterberg uses trials of reaction, attention, and skill as his tools. Readers get a founding text of industrial psychology, written with brisk confidence.
rosalynde-or-euphues-golden-legacy: Thomas Lodge's Rosalynde, or Euphues' Golden Legacy, is presented here in a school edition from Ginn and Company. Edward Chauncey Baldwin, professor of English literature at the University of Illinois, edited the book with an introduction and notes. His copyright of 1910 stands on the edition, which belongs to the Standard English Classics series. The contents page shown begins with Baldwin's introduction, at page seven of the front matter. No page of Lodge's own text, and no list beyond that first entry, is printed in the pages at hand.
round-about-rambles-in-lands-of-fact-and: Frank R. Stockton wrote Round-About Rambles in Lands of Fact and Fancy, in a new edition issued in New York in 1910 by Charles Scribner's Sons. The work had been entered for copyright in 1872. The contents list short pieces that mix fact and fancy, among them Winter in the Woods, Tricks of Light, Saving the Toll, and The Real King of Beasts.
shakspere-and-montaigne-an-endeavour-to-:
Jacob Feis wrote this study of Hamlet's bent of mind, traced through hints in works of Shakespeare's own time. Contents set the frame: the beginnings of English drama, the stage as a ground for political and religious fights, and Shakespeare's political creed. John Florio's English version of Montaigne's essays gets its own place.

Later parts treat Montaigne himself, then Hamlet, then the stage war between Ben Jonson and Dekker. Feis alleges a dispute and a skirmish between Jonson and Shakespeare, with Poetaster as a weapon. Readers get a bold period reading of Hamlet as a child of Montaigne's doubt.
sienkiewicz-the-knights-of-the-cross-krz:
Henryk Sienkiewicz set The Knights of the Cross in medieval Poland, and English readers follow its wars and loves here. Poland's knights face the feared Teutonic Order along a tense border. The long clash builds toward the great Battle of Grunwald in 1410.

Love stories thread through raids, sieges, and court intrigue. Young Zbyszko's vow, pride, and passion drive much of the tale. Sienkiewicz, a Nobel laureate, wrote to stir Polish pride under foreign rule. The novel blends romance and national epic, and it remains his most Polish book, loved at home for over a century.
temporal-power-a-study-in-supremacy: Marie Corelli wrote Temporal Power, subtitled A Study in Supremacy. The novel's chapter list opens with The King's Pleasaunce. Majesty Considers and Resolves comes next. A Nation or a Church follows. Later titles name The King's Double and The King's Veto. Of the Corruption of the State stands near the end. The Scorn of Kings closes the parts shown. The list runs past twenty chapters in all.
the-bedford-row-conspiracy:
William Makepeace Thackeray built his tale, by his own note, on a story by Charles de Bernard. Chapter one concerns the loves of Mr Perkins and Miss Gorgon and two great factions in the town of Oldborough. Later chapters show a plot thickening near Bedford Row and move behind the scenes.

Lucy and John argue over where to live, weighing Doughty Street, taxes, servants, and a house at Chelsea with a garden and greenhouse. Lucy fears an unlit road, public houses, and being left alone all day. John answers with fond protests. Domestic bargaining, town rivalry, and a coming plot are joined from the first talk.
the-centralia-conspiracy:
Ralph Chaplin wrote this booklet about the Armistice Day tragedy in Centralia, Washington. On November 11, 1919, four American Legion men were killed by members of the Industrial Workers of the World. Chaplin opens with a passage from Emerson on martyrs, then a section headed Murder or Self-Defense?

He states at once that the booklet is no apology for murder. Taking life, he holds, can be justified only in self-defense, and even then it marks a fall toward savagery. A nation worthy of the name civilization, he argues, must settle human disputes by means other than bloodshed. His aim is to untangle the chain of events that led to the killings, against the account given by the capitalist press. Readers get a defense-side history of a case that shocked the country.
the-commission-in-lunacy:
Honore de Balzac wrote this tale, translated here by Clara Bell and dedicated to the Contre-Amiral Bazoche, governor of the Isle of Bourbon. The scene opens in Paris in 1828, at about one in the morning. Two men come out of a large house in the Rue du Faubourg Saint-Honore, near the Elysee-Bourbon.

One is the famous doctor Horace Bianchon, and the other is Eugene de Rastignac, among the most elegant men in Paris, and the two are old friends. Rastignac proposes walking as far as the boulevard, where a cab can always be found at the club till daybreak. Their talk turns on a woman they have just left, the Marquise d'Espard. Bianchon speaks of her coldly, as if she were a hospital case, and warns his friend against swapping Madame de Nucingen for her. The lunacy commission of the title grows from that household.
the-meaning-of-infancy:
John Fiske's The Meaning of Infancy appeared in 1883 and was reprinted in the Riverside Educational Monographs, a series edited by Henry Suzzallo. The volume joins two essays: the title piece from Fiske's Excursions of an Evolutionist. A second essay treats the part played by infancy in the evolution of man, from A Century of Science. Fiske opens with a plain question about human helplessness at birth.

Man alone among animals, Fiske notes, shows a capacity for progress, yet man is born more helpless than any other creature. He argues the two facts are connected deep in the processes of evolution. Progressiveness and a long infancy, he says, are two sides of one and the same fact. The lengthening of infancy gradually converted brute ancestors into human beings. Readers get a short, clear statement of Fiske's famous claim that babyhood made man what he is.
the-prospective-mother-a-handbook-for-wo: J. Morris Slemons, associate professor of obstetrics at Johns Hopkins, wrote The Prospective Mother for women without medical knowledge. His preface aims to answer the questions pregnancy raises and to prevent serious complications. Treatment, he says, belongs to a physician who can observe the patient, and mothers should be under supervision throughout pregnancy. He retells his teacher J. Whitridge Williams's textbook, as he puts it, in words of one syllable, with a glossary for technical terms. The pages provided hold the preface only.
the-purpose-of-the-papacy:
John S. Vaughan, Bishop of Sebastopolis, argues for the papacy in a volume issued at London in 1910 by Sands and Company, with an introduction written at his urging by a fellow bishop. A motto from J. K. Stone insists that a Church of God either existed at the start of the sixteenth century or did not.

From that premise Vaughan contends the Reformers could neither rightly leave such a Church nor remake it. The introduction praises his earlier devotional and controversial books and frames the present one for general readers. Catholic readers and students of Reformation debate both find a direct, confessional case stated in compact form.
the-red-conspiracy: Joseph J. Mereto published his warning against socialism with the National Historical Society at New York in 1920, and the publisher urges loyal Americans to place it in every home, school, and library. A detailed contents analysis promises value to workingmen, sympathy for labor, and quotations from socialist authorities, while arguing that revolution sets labor back. Here only the publisher's appeal and opening of the analytical contents are present, so the argument itself does not appear.
the-rise-of-the-democracy: Joseph Clayton published his history with Cassell in 1911, with eight plates including King John granting Magna Carta. Contents begin with early struggles against crown absolutism, naming Anselm, Becket against Henry the Second, Langton against John, and the Great Charter, then turn to the beginning of parliamentary representation. Here only the title pages and opening of the contents list are present, so the history itself does not appear.
the-war-and-democracy:
R. W. Seton-Watson, J. Dover Wilson, Alfred E. Zimmern, and Arthur Greenwood wrote The War and Democracy, dated 1915 and dedicated to the Workers' Educational Association. Verses by Ebenezer Elliott ask when God will save the people, answering not kings and lords but nations and men. A Mazzini line from 1832 calls remaking Europe's map around peoples' missions the first essential step.

The material present here stops at the start of the contents, so the essays themselves do not appear. Chapter one is an introduction by Zimmern, late fellow and tutor of New College, Oxford, and author of The Greek Commonwealth. Readers get the book's democratic wartime programme from its dedications and mottoes.
thirty-years-in-the-itinerancy:
The Rev. W. G. Miller, D.D., published Thirty Years in the Itinerancy in 1875 and dedicated it to the ministers and laymen of the Wisconsin Conference. An itinerancy means a minister's circuit of travelling appointments. Miller prepared the pages amid heavy ministerial work and recent severe illness.

His preface explains the plan: a short record of the Wisconsin Conference's charges and ministers, following the line of his own thirty years of labour. Some prepared material had to be left out for length. Readers get church history meant to preserve facts for future historians.
